To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the N-terminus controls RGS protein stability and expression in human embryonic 293 cells and that a novel RGS mutation (Q2L) with decreased protein expression is relevant to the pathogenesis of hypertension in humans.
the expression of RGS proteins can be controlled by proteasomal degradation and that this regulation is important for the function of RGS2 and RGS4 in human embryonic renal 293 cells.
the N termini of RGS proteins are critical for protein stability and function, and a novel R4 subfamily mutation (RGS2Q2L) is associated with decreased protein expression in HEK 293 cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the N-terminal residues in controlling the proteasomal degradation of the RGS2, 3, 4, 5, and 8 in human embryonic 293 cells.
the role of N-terminal residues in regulating RGS2, 4, and 5 expression and function and the relevance to hypertension in humans.
the role of RGS proteins in the regulation of G protein-coupling receptor (GPCR)-signaling and the role of R4 subfamiliy proteins in the control of blood pressure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
N-terminal residues control RGS2, 4, and 5 expression in HEK-293 cells, but that the N terminus of RGS8 does not control its expression.
RGS2 and RGS8 are regulated by the proteasome and that RGS4 and RGS5 are regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.

the N termini of RGS proteins play a key role in controlling protein expression in HEK cells and that this mechanism can be exploited to alter function and expression of RGS4, -5 and possibly other family members.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the N terminus of RGS proteins is critical for protein expression, that RGS4 and RGS5 are not regulated by the N terminus, and that RGS2 and RGS8 are regulated by the N-terminal residues.
RGS2, 3, 4, 5, 8 are all regulated at the protein level and that RGS2 is the only RGS protein that has been shown to have receptor specificity.
N-terminal residues control proteasomal degradation of RGS2 (and possibly RGS4 and RGS5) in human embryonic 293 cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the N terminus is a key regulator of RGS protein expression in human embryonic cells.
the N terminus of RGS4-family RGS proteins plays an important role in regulating protein stability.
the N terminus of the RGS proteins is critical in controlling their expression and function, which in turn is critical for the regulation of GPCR signaling.
